text: Two of the most upvoted reviews on this Steam demo say the same thing. It's a crypto miner. Don't install it.
It isn't. But I know why they think that, and it's sitting in the game's own file list.
This is Nomad Drive. You repair a rundown RV and drive it across a procedurally generated wasteland, alone or with up to three friends.
The demo went up on June fifteenth. Right now, while I'm recording this, about two thousand people are inside it.
Seven hundred ninety four recent reviews, seventy one percent positive. Steam calls that Mostly Positive.
The number that made me pick this one: the median reviewer had two hours and thirty six minutes on it before they wrote anything.
Two and a half hours, in a free demo. Nobody is bouncing off this. Some of them just think it's mining crypto while they play.
Those two things have the same cause, and I can show you, because Steam publishes a file list for every demo.
Three hundred and twenty two entries. Three point seven gigabytes. No unpacking, no decompiling, nothing private. Just names and sizes.
Start with the engine. The first line is already odd.
It's Unity. But it's the High Definition Render Pipeline, and there's a GPU driven runtime in there too, which puts it on Unity six.
Almost every small team picks the Universal pipeline instead. It's lighter and it runs on anything. HDRP looks better and costs more to run.
Which brings us back to the crypto miner. There is no miner in that file list. What there is, is a very expensive renderer and, apparently, nothing capping the frame rate.
Players reported ninety nine percent GPU load sitting in the menu. On a five thousand series card. Doing nothing.
That's what an uncapped render loop looks like from outside. Your fans spin up on a menu screen, and you assume something is stealing from you.
So that's the look. What about the driving, which is the entire point of the game?
They licensed it. Vehicle Physics two, its wheel controller, and the multiplayer add on that ships with it.
Which is the right call. Writing a vehicle simulator is a year of your life, easily. Nobody should be doing that twice.
Same story for the world. The terrain is MapMagic two, a node graph that generates the map at runtime.
That explains a complaint that shows up over and over in the Chinese reviews. It gets repetitive a few hours in.
And there are only four scenes in the whole build, the biggest one half a megabyte. The gigabytes are all loot and locations, streamed in.
Then the co-op, which is where a small team usually drowns.
Mirror, which is free and open source, running over the Epic Online Services relay, with Steam lobbies next to it and Vivox for voice.
Server bill, zero. That shows up in the reviews too. Two players in the same city, five kilometres apart, getting three to four hundred milliseconds.
That's not a bug in their code. That's what a free global relay does. Your traffic goes wherever the relay happens to be.
So the driving is bought, the world is bought, the netcode is bought. What did they actually build?
Sixteen assemblies of their own. Dependency injection, save system, localization, input, audio, settings, and the glue over Mirror.
That is a studio framework. Whoever is behind Indie Devil has shipped software before.
Although they also shipped a folder that Unity itself names Do Not Ship, and left every asset package's sample code in the build.
That's what shipping fast looks like. In the reviews, driving is what people talk about most, and performance is what they complain about loudest.
And the split is telling. Positive reviewers had played three hours and eighteen minutes. Negative reviewers, one hour and twelve.
The word potential shows up in fifty positive reviews and two negative ones. People aren't asking for a finished game. They want it to run.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Unity six on HDRP. Team size never disclosed. Public devlogs going back to twenty twenty four. Mirror, Epic Online Services, MapMagic, and Vehicle Physics two.
And the trick, if you want one: they licensed every hard system and spent their own time on the glue and the content.
Worth a dip. Early access is set for September thirtieth, and the demo is free right now.
If you're shipping a demo this year, the lesson costs you one afternoon. Cap your frame rate in the menu, or the internet will decide you're a miner.
Next time, another demo, another file list. This is Demo Dip.
